title: Individual assignment 2
text:
Instructions

Make the repository. Create a public GitHub.com repository under your personal account, named dsci522-dockerfile-practice, with a README. Clone it; everything below happens in this folder.
Make a small project with uv or renv, whichever you prefer. Install these two packages, each pinned to an exact version (commands below): cowsay and numpy for uv, or cowsay and praise for renv. The test in step 4 loads exactly these two, so it fails if either is missing.

uv: pyproject.toml lists each package with ==, and Python 3.11 or newer is pinned in .python-version. Commit pyproject.toml, uv.lock and .python-version, but not .venv/.
renv: a small script hello.R uses both packages, and a snapshot records their exact versions in renv.lock. Commit hello.R, renv.lock, .Rprofile and renv/ (the .gitignore inside renv/ keeps the installed packages out).

Add the Dockerfile. Copy the uv or renv version below into a file named Dockerfile (no file extension) in the root of your repository. It installs your packages exactly as your lock file records them. The comments explain each line. For renv, change 4.6.2 on the FROM line to the R version in your renv.lock.
Test it on your computer. Build the image, then load your packages in a container from it (commands below). Fix problems now: debugging on your computer is much faster than on GitHub Actions.
Publish with GitHub Actions. Set up Docker Hub and the two secrets (see below). Then copy the workflow below into .github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml as it is: no changes needed. Commit and push.
Check that it worked. The run on the Actions tab finishes with a green check mark, and your Docker Hub repository shows two tags: latest and sha- plus 7 characters.







TipCommands to make the project (step 2)





Run these in the terminal, from your repository folder.

uv (Python)renv (R)


# 1. Start a uv project and pin the Python version
uv init --bare
uv python pin 3.14

# 2. Open pyproject.toml to tell uv to pin exact versions
nano pyproject.toml
Add these two lines at the bottom of pyproject.toml, then exit and save the file (in nano: Ctrl+X to exit, then Y to save):


pyproject.toml

[tool.uv]
add-bounds = "exact"

# 3. Install both packages: uv writes them with == in pyproject.toml
uv add cowsay numpy

# 4. Keep the .venv/ folder out of Git
echo ".venv/" >> .gitignore

# 5. Commit and push
git add pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version .gitignore
git commit -m "Add uv project with cowsay and numpy"
git push


# 1. Start an empty renv project
Rscript -e 'renv::init(bare = TRUE)'

# 2. Install both packages
Rscript -e 'renv::install(c("cowsay", "praise"))'
Then create a file named hello.R that uses both packages. renv::snapshot() only records packages your code loads, so without it renv.lock stays empty.


hello.R

library(cowsay)
library(praise)

say(praise())

# 3. Record the exact versions in renv.lock
Rscript -e 'renv::snapshot()'

# 4. Commit and push
git add hello.R renv.lock .Rprofile renv/
git commit -m "Add renv project with cowsay and praise"
git push
If the terminal says Rscript: command not found (common in Git Bash on Windows), run the part inside the quotes in the R console instead, from your repository folder.












TipThe Dockerfile (step 3)






uv (Python)renv (R)




Dockerfile

# Adapted from docker-uv-renv by Daniel Chen (MIT License)
# https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv

# Start from Ubuntu Linux. It has no Python: uv installs it.
FROM ubuntu:24.04

# Copy the uv program into the image (0.13.7 pins uv's version)
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/

# Work in the /workspace folder inside the image
WORKDIR /workspace

# Put the packages in /opt/venv (not in a .venv folder in /workspace)
ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv

# Copy only the files that list your packages
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./

# Install Python and the exact packages in uv.lock
# (--locked: stop if uv.lock doesn't match pyproject.toml)
RUN uv sync --locked





Dockerfile

# Adapted from docker-uv-renv by Daniel Chen (MIT License)
# https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv

# Start from Ubuntu Linux with R installed.
# Change 4.6.2 to the R version in your renv.lock.
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2

# Install curl: renv downloads packages with it
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install --yes curl

# Work in the /workspace folder inside the image
WORKDIR /workspace

# Put the packages in /opt/renv/library (not in renv/library in /workspace)
RUN echo "RENV_PATHS_LIBRARY=/opt/renv/library" >> /usr/local/lib/R/etc/Renviron.site

# Copy the files renv needs to install your packages, and your script
COPY renv.lock .Rprofile hello.R ./
COPY renv/activate.R renv/

# Install the exact packages in renv.lock
RUN Rscript -e "renv::restore()"













TipCommands to test your image (step 4)





Open Docker Desktop first. From your repository folder, build the image and give it a name (--tag):
docker build --tag dsci522-test .
Then start a container, use your two packages, and remove the container when it finishes (--rm). If a cow talks to you, it worked: an error means a package didn’t install.

uv (Python)renv (R)


docker run --rm dsci522-test uv run python -c \
  "import cowsay, numpy; cowsay.cow(f'numpy says 1 + 2 + 3 = {numpy.sum([1, 2, 3])}')"


docker run --rm dsci522-test Rscript -e \
  "library(cowsay); library(praise); say(praise())"



Changed your environment? Run docker build again: Docker rebuilds only the steps that changed.









TipThe workflow file (step 5)





Copy it as it is: it reads your Docker Hub username from the DOCKER_USERNAME secret. The comments explain the rest.


.github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml

# Builds the image from your Dockerfile and publishes it on Docker Hub.
# Save this file as .github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml

name: Publish image to Docker Hub

# When the workflow runs
on:
  # by hand: Actions tab > Publish image to Docker Hub > Run workflow
  workflow_dispatch:
  # on its own: when a push changes one of these files
  push:
    paths:
      - Dockerfile
      - uv.lock
      - renv.lock
      - .github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml

env:
  # The image name: your Docker Hub username (from the secret) / repository name
  IMAGE: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/dsci522-dockerfile-practice

jobs:
  publish:
    # a fresh Linux computer on GitHub (Intel/AMD)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      # 1. Copy your repository onto that computer
      - name: Check out the repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # 2. Log in to Docker Hub with your two repository secrets
      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}

      # 3. Build the image with two tags:
      #    latest, and sha- plus the first 7 characters of the commit ID
      - name: Build the image
        run: docker build --tag "$IMAGE:latest" --tag "$IMAGE:sha-${GITHUB_SHA::7}" .

      # 4. Upload both tags to Docker Hub
      - name: Push the image
        run: docker push --all-tags "$IMAGE"

Steps 3 and 4 are the same docker build and docker push you would type on your own computer: GitHub just runs them for you, from the files in your repository.









TipSetting up Docker Hub and the GitHub secrets (step 5)






Create a free Docker Hub account if you don’t have one.
You don’t need to create the Docker Hub repository: the workflow’s first push creates it. Afterwards, check on Docker Hub that it is public.
Create a Docker Hub access token with Read & Write permissions. Copy it somewhere safe: you can only see it once.
In your GitHub repository, add two repository secrets (Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions > New repository secret), with exactly these names, because the workflow looks for them:

DOCKER_USERNAME: your Docker Hub username (not your GitHub username)
DOCKER_PASSWORD: the access token (not your Docker Hub password)











TipTroubleshooting






Git refuses to push the workflow file: your personal access token needs the workflow scope. On GitHub, go to Settings > Developer settings > Personal access tokens, select your token, and tick workflow.
The workflow didn’t start: it only starts on its own when a push changes the Dockerfile, a lock file or the workflow file. Run it by hand: Actions tab > Publish image to Docker Hub > Run workflow.
The login step fails: check the secret names, and that DOCKER_PASSWORD is an access token with Read & Write permissions.
The push step fails with “denied” or “unauthorized”: the DOCKER_USERNAME secret must be your Docker Hub username, all in lowercase.
The logs show *** instead of your username: that’s normal. GitHub hides every secret value in the logs.

text:
This optional bonus turns your whole project into a Quarto website on GitHub Pages, at the same URL as the report you published in Milestone 2.

Make your project’s _quarto.yml a website that renders into docs/
Add a homepage (your README), your report (HTML and PDF), an about page, and a GitHub icon in the menu bar
Make make all build everything, from downloading the data to the website
Publish it on GitHub Pages







ImportantUp to 5 bonus points, for your team



The points go to Milestone 4 unless you tell us otherwise when you submit. They can make up for points lost on that milestone, but can’t take it above its maximum. It is due with Milestone 4 (see the syllabus), and we grade it from the same 3.0.0 release, so your Milestone 4 README instructions must still work exactly as written.








TipReadings for this bonus

Quarto: includes and alt text for figures







Edit _quarto.yml in the root of your repository: add type: website and output-dir: docs, list the website’s pages under render, and add a website section with the menu bar (example below). Keep your existing format settings (such as embed-resources and PDF): they still apply to your report.
Give each new page format: html in its YAML header, so Quarto doesn’t also make a PDF of it.
Add an empty .nojekyll file to the root of your repository (Quarto copies it into docs/), and add .quarto/ to your .gitignore.
Clean up the old report: it now renders to docs/reports/<your-report>.html and .pdf, with the website’s menu bar. Delete the old rendered files from reports/, and update your Makefile and README to the new locations.

quarto render now renders the whole website; quarto render reports/<your-report>.qmd still renders just the report, and quarto preview shows the website as you edit.






TipExample _quarto.yml and folder layout (step 1)





Change the title, the report’s file name and the repository URL to your own.


_quarto.yml

project:
  type: website
  output-dir: docs
  render:          # keeps files like CONTRIBUTING.md out of the website
    - index.qmd
    - about.qmd
    - reports/<your-report>.qmd

website:
  title: "Your project title"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: reports/<your-report>.qmd
        text: Report
      - href: about.qmd
        text: About
    right:
      - icon: github
        href: https://github.com/UBC-MDS-2026-27/<your-repository>
        aria-label: GitHub repository

# Keep your existing `format:` settings below.

Only the new and changed parts are shown:
.
├── _quarto.yml           # now a website: renders everything into docs/
├── .nojekyll
├── Makefile
├── README.md
├── index.qmd             # homepage: includes README.md
├── about.qmd             # the team
├── reports/
│   └── <your-report>.qmd
└── docs/                 # the published website (generated, but committed)
    ├── index.html
    └── reports/
        ├── <your-report>.html
        └── <your-report>.pdf







Homepage (index.qmd): include your README instead of copying it, so the homepage stays up to date. It needs no title: Quarto uses the README’s first heading.


index.qmd

---
format: html
---

{{< include README.md >}}

About page (about.qmd): for each team member, their name linked to their GitHub profile, and a few sentences in their own words (for example, their background and what interests them in data science). The site is public, so each person decides what to share. A photo is optional.
Report: the Report menu item links to its HTML page, and Quarto adds a link to the PDF on that page. Link to both versions from your README too. Give every figure alt text: the fig-alt option on code cells that make figures, or the fig-alt attribute on images:
![Feature densities.](../results/figures/densities.png){#fig-densities fig-alt="Density plots of each feature by class."}







WarningLinks in your README must work on the website too



The website only publishes its pages, not the rest of your repository. A relative link such as CONTRIBUTING.md or src/ works on GitHub but breaks on the website, and Quarto doesn’t warn you. Use the full GitHub URL instead (for example, https://github.com/UBC-MDS-2026-27/<your-repository>/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).





Extend your Milestone 4 Makefile so that make all, from a fresh clone inside your container, downloads the data, runs your validation checks and the rest of the analysis, then renders the whole website into docs/. make clean removes everything make all creates, including docs/.

Change the rule behind publish so it runs quarto render instead of copying the report (sketch below).
Remove your old rule that renders the report in reports/: the report now renders as part of the website.
List as prerequisites every file the website reads, including your README and the figures and tables your report shows.
Say in your README how to build the website.







TipSketch of the Makefile changes (step 3)





Change the file names to your own:


Makefile

.DELETE_ON_ERROR:

publish: docs/index.html

docs/index.html: _quarto.yml index.qmd README.md about.qmd \
        reports/<your-report>.qmd results/figures/<your-figure>.png
    quarto render

clean:
    rm -rf docs
    # ... and everything else your pipeline creates


quarto render empties docs/ first, so no old pages are left over.
.DELETE_ON_ERROR: deletes docs/index.html if the render fails partway. Without it, the next make would find docs/index.html and say there is nothing to do.










ImportantA clean build, with no warnings



Before you submit, run make clean and then make all inside your container. Everything should rebuild, and Quarto should print no ERROR or WARN messages (for example, about links it could not find). Messages from other tools, such as Jupyter, don’t count. We grade the bonus by doing the same.

Policies

Academic Integrity
Academic integrity is a commitment to honesty, respect, responsibility, and accountability in academic work. It is foundational to teaching and learning and is a shared value of all members of the UBC community. In a project course, it also means being transparent with your teammates and the teaching team about how your work was produced.
Academic integrity in this course includes:

Submitting individual assignments that reflect your own understanding and intellectual contribution.
Contributing your fair share to your group’s project, and making sure your commits, pull requests, and reviews honestly represent the work you did.
Citing any code, text, or ideas you draw on from elsewhere (classmates outside your group, documentation, Stack Overflow, blog posts, generative AI tools, etc.), following the MDS program policy.
Respecting the licenses of any code, data, or other material you reuse in your project.
Following the generative AI policy below, including disclosing AI use for every deliverable.



Use of Generative AI
This course follows the MDS program’s Academic Integrity and Use of Generative AI policy. Assessment-specific instructions always take precedence over the general guidance below.
AI assistance is allowed. Generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, GitHub Copilot, Cursor) are a real part of modern data science workflows, and you may use them in this course to brainstorm, explain concepts, debug errors, or help write code and documentation. That said, this course is about building your own skills in version control, environments, containers, testing, and pipelines. We strongly encourage you to attempt the work yourself first, and to use AI to support your learning rather than replace it. A useful question to ask yourself is: is this tool helping me understand the problem, or is it doing the thinking I am here to learn to do?
Disclose your AI use. For every milestone and individual assignment, you must state whether generative AI was used, including when it was not. If AI was used, please share:

which tool(s) and model(s) you used;
which parts of the work they were used for, and how; and
the instructions you gave the tool, such as any system prompt or agent configuration file (e.g., CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursor/rules/, .github/copilot-instructions.md), or, if you did not use one, a few representative example prompts.

For group milestones, please keep this disclosure in an AI_USAGE.md file or CLAUDE.md (or other file names that indicate AI was used) in the root of your project repository and update it as the project evolves. For individual assignments, include the disclosure with your Gradescope submission. Disclosing AI use is not penalized, and it helps us give you useful feedback.
You remain responsible for everything you submit. Whether code was written by you, a teammate, or an AI tool, everyone in the group is responsible for its correctness, quality, and licensing. You should be able to explain what your code does, why it is designed that way, and how it fits into the rest of your project. Please do not merge code you have not read and understood.
Humans open pull requests and issues, and make the final merge decisions. AI agents may help you review or generate some code, and may help double-check code before pull requests are merged (e.g., an automated review bot such as Cursor Bugbot or GitHub Copilot code review), but a group member must review any generated changes and open every pull request and issue themselves. Ultimately, it is human reviewers who make the final decisions and merge the pull requests. Please do not let an AI agent push to your repository, open pull requests or issues, or merge pull requests on its own. Because GitHub history is used to evaluate teamwork, it should accurately reflect who did the work.
Communicate in your own words. When writing issues, pull request descriptions, code reviews, peer reviews, and team work reflections, please use your own words. AI may help with translation or grammar editing. Much of what you learn in this course comes from these conversations with your teammates.
Weekly check-ins. As described in Deliverables, the teaching team will have a short, ungraded oral check-in with each of you during lab every week, as practice for technical interviews. We may ask you to walk us through any part of your project, including code that was written with the help of AI. If someone is not yet able to explain work they contributed, we will follow up to better understand how the work was produced and to support their learning. Where needed, this may also include steps under UBC’s academic misconduct procedures.
Protect private information. Do not share confidential, private, or sensitive information with AI tools, including personal information about yourself, your teammates, or other students (for example, peer review content or team work reflections).
If you are unsure whether a particular use of AI is appropriate, please ask the teaching team before you submit your work.
Academic misconduct
Violations of academic integrity (i.e., academic misconduct) may lead to serious consequences. For more details, please see UBC’s Academic Integrity website, the Academic Calendar Statement on Academic Misconduct, and UBC’s guidance on Generative AI.

text:
This assignment will provide practice in the context of version control and will prepare you to collaborate on your group projects for this course. Follow the instructions listed below. You will be graded for completion.

Create a new public repository on GitHub.com named learning-about-version-control. Make sure the repository:

Includes a README.md that has a heading that says “Learning about Version Control” and has your name listed as the author.








Importantgithub.com not https://github.ubc.ca/



Make sure you do this in your own personal public GitHub account. Do not make this in the UBC github.



Clone your learning-about-version-control repository to your local computer.
Create and resolve a merge conflict 😱!

On GitHub.com, open your README.md, click the pencil (edit) icon, and add a line that says “Solving merge conflicts is easy!”. Commit the change on GitHub.
On your local computer (without pulling first!), add a line in the same place in the README, but this time write “Solving merge conflicts is soooooo hard!”
Add and commit your local changes to the README.md, then try to push. Git will reject the push, because GitHub has a commit you don’t have locally yet.
Pull the changes from GitHub with git pull --no-rebase. This is when the merge conflict appears. (The --no-rebase tells git to merge the two versions. Without it, newer versions of git stop and ask you how to combine them.)
Resolve the merge conflict on your local computer so that the line reads “Solving merge conflicts takes conscious effort, but I can do it!”. Take a screenshot while you are resolving the conflict (with the conflict markers <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>> visible) to show you did this.
Add and commit the resolved file, then push to your remote repository on GitHub.com.

Create and accept a pull request!

Create a new Git branch on your local version control repository named opinions and switch to that branch.
Edit your README.md so that you add at least one sentence about what you like most about version control, and add at least one sentence about what you find most challenging/confusing/frustrating about version control (we all have opinions on this one…). Add and commit your changes to local version control.
Push the changes to the README.md that you made on the opinions branch to the remote repository on GitHub.com.
Visit GitHub.com and create a pull request to suggest that the changes on the opinions branch should be merged into the main branch.
Merge the pull request you opened, so your changes from the opinions branch go into the main branch.

On GitHub, go to Settings > Pages. Under Source pick Deploy from a branch, then pick the main branch and the /docs folder, and click Save.

Wait a few minutes and refresh: the page shows the link to your live report.










TipTroubleshooting






A YAML error when you render: indent with 2 spaces (not 4, not a tab), and put a : after every setting name.
A setting seems ignored: check it appears only once in the YAML header (e.g. no leftover format: html).
The reference list is empty: you haven’t cited anything yet. Add [@key] citations in the text.
@fig-... or @tbl-... shows as “?@fig-…”: labels must start with fig- or tbl- and use -, not _ (fig-horse-pop, not horse_pop).
The PDF fails but the HTML works: read the error message for the line number, and check special characters in your captions.

title: Milestone 1
text:
Milestone 1 summary
In this milestone, you will:

Draft a teamwork contract
Set up a public GitHub repository in the course organization, with its required metadata
Create an appropriate file and directory structure for a data analysis project
Write the data analysis as a Quarto document (.qmd)
Make the computational environment reproducible with a virtual environment (uv or renv). Hint: do this as you create the analysis, don’t wait until the end!

An example Milestone 1 that corresponds to our expectations from this year is here: Breast Cancer Predictor in Python 0.0.1

1. Draft a teamwork contract
This document will govern the working relationships on your team, and if done correctly, it should help you manage and resolve any issues that might arise when working in a group. Start from the teamwork contract template, based on a contract from a past data science project: copy it into a Quarto document, make it your team’s own, and render it to PDF.
A teamwork contract communicates how the group will work together. It includes details about the logistics of working together, the expectations you have for each other, and how you plan to navigate conflicts.
Some aspects of the teamwork contract could be:

How will work be distributed in a fair and equitable way?
What are the expected work hours for the project?
How often will group meetings occur?
Will you have meeting agendas and minutes? If so, what will be the system for rotating through these responsibilities?
What will be the style of working?

Will you start each day with stand-ups, or submit a summary of your contributions 4 hours before each meeting? or something else?

What is the quality of work each team member expects from themselves and each other?
When are team members not available (e.g., evenings and Sundays because of family obligations).
And any other similar things that govern your working relationships.

Use this opportunity to use your prior knowledge/experience to improve your teamwork, communication, leadership, and organizational skills. You will need all of these for your capstone projects (and beyond)! Please actually talk this through as a team and fill it in with care. A contract that is clearly rushed or left mostly as the template will lose marks.

Note - this document is fairly personal and does NOT need to reside in your public GitHub.com repo. Instead you can prove that you created this by submitting a copy of it to Gradescope under the Milestone 1 assignment.



2. Set up a GitHub repository
After we add you to the UBC-MDS-2026-27 organization on GitHub.com, set up a public GitHub repository for your group under that organization (not under one of your personal accounts), and give your whole team access to it (see Repository metadata below). Once you have decided on a project question and data set, make sure your repository has a name that is relevant to that question. Note: if you need to change the name of your project repository later, you can!
We are using github.com and public repositories because we will eventually be using some fancy tooling (e.g., GitHub Actions) in this project. For this to work, all your work for this project (including scripts) should be developed and live in this repository on GitHub.com. Additionally, this will help you build a portfolio of your work you can share with others.

Repository metadata






ImportantThis metadata is used for the class automatons, and it is also worth points



Proper metadata setup is also graded, on top of the rest of this milestone. Metadata that is not fixed in week 1 (by the Milestone 1 deadline) will continue to lose points in each milestone until it is fixed.
Lab attendance is mandatory, and the teaching team is there with you. There is no reason for a username or metadata problem to be left unresolved, or at least undocumented, after your week 1 lab session.


Your group’s repository needs all three of the following:

It lives in the course organization. Create it in UBC-MDS-2026-27, not under a personal account or the UBC-MDS organization.
Its Description begins with DSCI 522. It must be literally these characters: capital DSCI, one space, 522, at the very start of the description. The rest of the description is up to your group; use it to say what your project is about. To edit it, click the gear icon next to About on your repository’s main page.

Correct: DSCI 522: Predicting wine quality from its chemistry
Incorrect: dsci 522 ..., DSCI522 ..., DSCI-522 ..., Predicting wine quality (DSCI 522), or a description with a space before DSCI 522

It is added to two teams: 522-students, and your group’s own team.



Team
Where to check it
Role to give it




522-students
https://github.com/orgs/UBC-MDS-2026-27/teams/522-students/repositories
Read


your group’s team, 522-team-XX
e.g., group 1’s is https://github.com/orgs/UBC-MDS-2026-27/teams/522-team-01/repositories
Admin



Your group’s team is named 522-team- followed by your group number as two digits: group 1 is 522-team-01, group 12 is 522-team-12. To find it, go to the organization, open Teams, click 522-students, and your group’s team is listed under it as a sub-team.
To add the teams, open your repository’s Settings → Collaborators and teams → Add teams, search for the team, and pick the role in the table. You need admin access to the repository to see this page; whoever created the repository has it. Giving your group’s team the Admin role gives every member of your group admin access too, which you will need later (e.g., to add GitHub secrets in Milestone 2).
When you are done, open both team links: your repository should be listed under each team’s Repositories tab.

Every member of your group also needs all three of the following. Each member should check their own:

You are a member of the organization. Accept your invitation to UBC-MDS-2026-27: it is in your email, or at https://github.com/orgs/UBC-MDS-2026-27/invitation.
You are a member of 522-students and of your group’s 522-team-XX sub-team. Check that you are listed under the Members tab of each, e.g., for group 1:

https://github.com/orgs/UBC-MDS-2026-27/teams/522-students/members
https://github.com/orgs/UBC-MDS-2026-27/teams/522-team-01/members

Your GitHub.com username is listed correctly in the lab sections file. It must match the username on your github.com profile exactly, and you must be listed in the right group.

Check all of this during your week 1 lab session. If any of it is wrong for you (an invitation you can’t find, a team you are not in, or a missing or misspelled username), raise it with the teaching team in that lab, so that it is either fixed there or documented as something still to fix.
Keep this metadata in place for the rest of the course. Renaming the repository is fine, but the description must keep starting with DSCI 522, and the repository must stay in both teams.



3. Create an appropriate file & directory structure for a data analysis project
For this project, you are expected to follow the best practices we have learned about in regards to project directory and file structures. For this milestone, your repository should look something like this. Include whichever of these files are relevant to your project: for example, the uv files if you use Python, the renv files if you use R, or both if you use both.
your-project-name/
├── README.md
├── CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
├── CONTRIBUTING.md
├── LICENSE.md
├── .gitignore
├── pyproject.toml          # Python (uv)
├── uv.lock                 # Python (uv)
├── .python-version         # Python (uv)
├── renv.lock               # R (renv)
├── .Rprofile               # R (renv)
├── renv/                   # R (renv): follow the .gitignore in here
├── data/
│   ├── raw/                # data exactly as downloaded
│   └── processed/          # cleaned / intermediate data
└── analysis/               # or reports/, src/
    ├── <descriptive-name>.qmd
    └── <descriptive-name>.html  # or .pdf
Keep the project root tidy: only the files above that are relevant to your project should live there. Put the analysis document in a sub-folder with a sensible name (e.g., analysis/, reports/), not in the root. Too many files in the root makes it hard for collaborators (including future you!) to find things.
Add a .gitignore so that system and temporary files never get committed. At minimum, it should ignore .DS_Store and .venv/.
The description of each file and folder follows.

i. README.md
The README.md lives in the root of your repository. It is the first thing people see, so it should tell a stranger what this project is and how to run it. Include:

Project title that matches your project topic.
Authors: the names of all team members.
Summary: a short paragraph (view from 10,000 feet) that says what question you asked, what you found at a high level, and 1-2 sentences on what the findings might mean.
How to run the analysis: step-by-step instructions that someone who has never seen your project can follow, from cloning the repo to rendering the report. Tell them how to set up the environment (e.g., uv sync) and which command to run. Don’t make the reader guess.
Dependencies: list them (e.g., uv, Quarto) or link to where they are listed (e.g., pyproject.toml).
Licenses: the names of the licenses in LICENSE.md (e.g., MIT and CC BY-NC-ND 4.0).
AI use statement: say whether you used generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot) in this project. If you did, say how. If you used instruction files (e.g., CLAUDE.md, a system prompt file), commit them to the repo and point to them. Also include a few example prompts.
Link to the rendered report (e.g., your GitHub Pages URL).

Click every link in your README to make sure it works, and proofread for spelling and grammar.


ii. CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
In an attempt to create a safe, positive, productive, and happy community, many organizations and developers create a code of conduct for their projects. A code of conduct in a Data Science project informs others of social norms, acceptable behaviour and general etiquette. It is more outward facing than the teamwork contract discussed above. We recommend Project Include for a comprehensive guide to writing an effective Code of Conduct.
At minimum, we believe that a good/effective code of conduct should include:

A statement on diversity and inclusivity
Details on expected, and unacceptable behaviour
A list of consequences for unacceptable behaviour
A procedure for reporting and dealing with unacceptable behaviour

It is fine to adapt an existing code of conduct, but you must cite the original source (its name and a link) in the file. If you adapt one, update the contact email in the reporting/enforcement section so it reaches your team, not the original project. Proofread it.

Sample Codes of Conduct:

idocde Coc
Python Community CoC
Tidyverse CoC
Pandas CoC
Vox Media CoC

Note - this document should live in the root of your public GitHub.com repository.



iii. CONTRIBUTING.md
It is a good practice to include information about how others, outside the core team, can contribute to your project somewhere in your repository. This is typically done as a separate file in the repository called CONTRIBUTING.md. After reading it, someone should know how to report a bug, suggest a change, and submit their work (e.g., open an issue, make a branch, open a pull request). Here are some examples of this file:

Altair
dplyr
Atom editor (very comprehensive)
AI fairness research paper

Your CONTRIBUTING.md is also required to have an AI policy section. It tells contributors whether and how they may use generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Copilot, Claude) when they contribute to your project: what is allowed, what they must disclose, and who is responsible for the result. Your policy must be consistent with this course’s expectations (see Expectations: pull requests and issues are opened, reviewed and merged by you, not by an AI agent). Here are some examples of AI policies from open source projects:

earthaccess
SciPy
SymPy

Same rule as the code of conduct: if you adapt any of these, cite the original source. Fill in every section (no leftover template placeholders) and check that all links work.
Note - this document should live in the root of your public GitHub.com repository.


iv. data/
The data/ folder should contain a copy of the downloaded data, and it should get written there by code in your analysis (not downloaded by hand). Keep raw data and processed data separate: put the data exactly as you downloaded it in data/raw/, and anything you clean or create from it in data/processed/.
An exception can be made if the data set is extremely large (> 100 MB per file). In that case, reach out to the instructional team to make an alternative plan, and explain in your README why the data is not in the repo.


v. analysis/<descriptive-name>.qmd
For this milestone, the analysis code and narration should be contained within a single Quarto document (.qmd). See section 4 for what goes inside it. A few rules for the file itself:

Put it in a sub-folder (e.g., analysis/), not the project root.
Give it a descriptive name related to your project (e.g., penguin-species-classification.qmd), not analysis.qmd.
Push both the source document AND the rendered version (HTML or PDF). If you render to HTML, set up GitHub Pages so the report is easy to read online, and put its URL in your README.
Keep only one report. Delete drafts and scratch files so it is obvious which document is the real one.
Make sure it renders without errors.



vi. pyproject.toml, uv.lock & .python-version (or the corresponding renv files)
These files let others recreate your computational environment. See section 5 for details.
Note - these files should live in the root of your public GitHub.com repository.


vii. LICENSE.md
Licenses tell others how they may (or may not) use your work. We will learn more about licenses later in the course, and for now we recommend using an MIT license for the project code and a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0) license for the project report. As long as your group agrees, these can be changed later in the course when you learn more about licenses. If you want to spend some time choosing different licenses now, we can recommend these two websites to help get you started:

https://choosealicense.com/
https://chooser-beta.creativecommons.org/

Your LICENSE.md needs:

Two licenses: one software license for the code (e.g., MIT) and one Creative Commons license for the report (e.g., CC BY-NC-ND 4.0).
The actual license text pasted into the file, not just a link to it.
The names of all team members in the copyright line.

The licenses named in your README should match the ones in LICENSE.md. Name the file exactly LICENSE.md.



4. Write the data analysis as a Quarto document
The content of this analysis project should be a narrated analysis that asks and answers a predictive or inferential question using a method you have already learned in MDS. For milestone 1, the code and analysis narrative should be contained within a single Quarto document (.qmd), using either Python or R code chunks.
Write it like a short scientific report. Your report should have the following sections:

Title
Summary: one paragraph that says what question you asked, what you found, and why it matters, plus the main limitations.
Introduction:

give enough background on the topic that someone unfamiliar with it can follow the rest of your report
explain why this problem is important or interesting. Don’t stop at one sentence; convince the reader it is worth answering.
clearly state the question you are trying to answer
describe the data set you used: where it comes from, what each row is, and which variables you use. Cite the data set.
clearly define your target/response variable (what you are predicting)
make sure your question can actually be answered with this data

Methods:

in written English, walk the reader through what you did from beginning to end, and why
name the model or method you used and explain why it fits your question
name the metric you used to evaluate it (e.g., accuracy, F1, RMSE) and explain why you chose it
your report should include code which:

downloads the data from its original source on the web and saves a copy to data/raw/
wrangles and cleans the data from its original (downloaded) format to the format needed for your analysis, and saves it to data/processed/
splits the data into training and test sets before doing any exploratory data analysis or preprocessing. Don’t break the golden rule of machine learning: the test set should not influence any decision you make.
summarizes the training data in a way that is relevant to your question (exploratory data analysis)
creates a visualization of the training data that is relevant to your question
performs the classification or regression analysis


Results:

show all the key results that answer your question, using figures and tables
make figures readable in the rendered HTML: label the axes in plain English (with units), include a legend when there is more than one colour or group, use a text size people can read, and avoid overplotting (e.g., with transparency)
keep tables clean: show the rows and columns that matter, with clear column names. Don’t dump a giant data frame.
give every figure and table a number and a caption (it’s ok to manually write down the figure/table number and caption for now, you do not need to use Quarto syntax for this yet), and refer to them in the text
double-check that what you say about the results matches what the figures and tables show

Discussion:

summarize what you found, and link it back to the question you asked
discuss what the findings mean in the real-world context of the problem (the domain)
discuss whether this is what you expected to find
discuss the assumptions and limitations of your methods and findings
discuss what impact such findings could have
discuss what future questions this could lead to

References:

at least 4 citations relevant to the project, including the data set (format is your choice, just be consistent across the references)
every reference in the list should be cited somewhere in the text
references should be actual peer-reviewed publications or reputable sources, not AI hallucinations!


A few writing rules that apply to the whole report:

Write in full sentences. Point form is OK in a few places, but most of your report should be paragraphs.
Don’t use code-style variable names in your writing. Write “flipper length”, not flipper_length_mm.
Spell out acronyms the first time you use them.
Proofread for spelling and grammar before you submit.

The analysis can be performed in either R or Python. The restrictions on the analysis methods and programming language are put in place to ensure that all group members can contribute equally to the project.
The data for the project should be publicly available, and clearly licensed to be shared and used openly on the internet. We strongly suggest you avoid using data sets where authentication is needed for access (e.g., Kaggle) as this adds another layer of complexity when making these projects reproducible. If you do use one, your README must walk the reader through every step of getting and setting up the API token.

Possible data set sources

City of Vancouver Open Data Portal
BC Data Catalogue
Government of Canada open data
GitHub repo of awesome public datasets
UCI Machine Learning Repository: Data Sets
tidytuesday data set
Google Data set search engine
fivethirtyeight R package (if you use this, see the note below!)

Note: if you choose a data set from the fivethirtyeight R package, you cannot copy their scientific question, visualizations or methods from the original FiveThirtyEight articles from where the data sets were first reported on. Finally, with the fivethirtyeight R package data sets, we want you to get practice reading them using the read_* functions in R or Python, so please use the versions of the data sets listed here: https://github.com/rudeboybert/fivethirtyeight/tree/master/data-raw



5. Make the computational environment reproducible
For this project, we will eventually be making the computation environment reproducible through containerization with Docker. For milestone 1 however, we will start with using a virtual environment as our first step towards this. Use one of:

uv (Python): Virtual environments: Python + uv (DSCI 521 notes)
renv (R): Virtual environments: R (DSCI 521 notes)







ImportantYour README instructions are worth 5 all-or-nothing points



5 points of this milestone are for the reproducibility of your README instructions: whether someone can follow them to set up your environment and run your analysis. These points are all-or-nothing. If your instructions do not work exactly as you have written them, you will lose all 5 points.
Make sure your instructions work on both Windows and Mac computers. If your team does not have both, work with another team to test them.

title: Milestone 1
text:
Expectations

Everyone should contribute equally to all aspects of the project (e.g., code, writing, project management). This should be evidenced by a roughly equal number of commits, pull request reviews and participation in communication via GitHub issues.
After the repository is set up, each group member should work in a GitHub flow workflow:

create a branch in your team’s repository (not a fork) for each feature or fix
give branches meaningful names that describe the work (e.g., add-eda-plot, not branch1 or alice)
keep each branch small: one independent piece of work, not half the project
open a pull request, and have at least one other teammate review it before it is merged. Don’t push straight to main.

You should be committing to git and pushing to GitHub.com every time you work on this project.
Git commit messages should be meaningful. These will be marked. It’s OK if one or two are less meaningful, but most should be.
Use GitHub issues to communicate with your teammates (as opposed to email or Slack). Use them for planning, splitting up tasks, and discussing decisions. We expect more than 3 issues per person on average.
Pull requests and issues must be opened by you, not by an AI agent or chat bot. You may use AI agents to help double-check code before merging pull requests, but ultimately it is human reviewers who make the final decisions and merge the pull requests.
Your question, analysis and visualization should make sense. It doesn’t have to be complicated.
You should use proper grammar and full sentences in your README and report. Point form may occur, but should be less than 10% of your written documents.

title: Milestone 3
text:
NoteThe end-of-course project goal





Your team answers a predictive question with a public data set, in R and/or Python, with a focus on reproducible and trustworthy workflows. By the end of the course, your single Quarto document will have become a project with:

well-documented, modular scripts in R and/or Python
a pipeline automated with GNU Make
a reproducible Quarto report
a Docker container for the computational environment
a GitHub repository for collaboration and sharing

title: Milestone 3
text:
Milestone 3 summary
This milestone is about moving your analysis code out of your report and into scripts, and checking your data before you use it.

Split your analysis into 4 or more scripts that take command line arguments
Add data validation checks to your scripts
Make your report a .qmd that shows the figures and tables your scripts saved, instead of computing them
Add any new packages to your environment and publish a new Docker image
Update your README so it says how to run each script in the container







ImportantSee what a finished Milestone 3 looks like



An example Milestone 3 that corresponds to our expectations is here: Breast Cancer Predictor 2.0.0. Look at its scripts/ folder and its README. It uses conda for its environment: ignore that part and keep the uv/renv setup from Milestone 2.








TipReadings for this milestone






Scripts: writing scripts with command line arguments (click and docopt)
Data validation: what to check, and the checklist you must cover
Data validation with pandera (Python) or with pointblank (R)





1. Move your code into scripts

Split your analysis into 4 or more scripts (.py or .R) in a scripts/ folder, one script per step of the analysis. The code doesn’t need to be turned into functions yet (that is Milestone 4). A common split:

download the data
clean and split the data
exploratory figures and tables
fit the model and evaluate it

Chain them: the files one script writes are the files the next script reads.
Give every script command line arguments for at least its input path and its output path, so nothing is hard-coded. Use click in Python, or docopt in R. Use descriptive file names (data/processed/cancer_train.csv, not data/file.csv).
Save every figure and table to a file (for example in results/), so the report can show it.







TipWhat each script could look like













Script
Reads
Writes




download
a URL
data/raw/...


clean and split
the raw data
cleaned train and test files in data/processed/


EDA
the training data
figures and tables in results/


model
the training and test data
the fitted model, plus result figures and tables in results/



Running a Python script in the container looks like this (R: Rscript instead of uv run python):
docker compose run --rm analysis-env \
  uv run python scripts/download_data.py \
  --url https://example.com/data.csv \
  --write-to data/raw/cancer.csv
You can split your code differently, or have more scripts. What matters is having about 4, so you can practise joining them into a pipeline in Milestone 4.





2. Add data validation checks

Write the checks as code in your scripts, for example in the script that cleans or splits the data.
Write at least one check for each item in the textbook’s data validation checklist.
Decide what happens when a check fails (stop with an error, or warn and continue), and make the code do that.
Don’t leak test data: checks that look at relationships between columns (such as correlations) run on the training data only.



3. Make your report show your scripts’ results

If your report is not a .qmd yet, convert it: quarto convert report.ipynb for a Jupyter notebook, or just rename an .Rmd file to .qmd.
Replace the analysis code in the report with code that reads and displays the figures and tables your scripts saved.
Don’t polish its formatting yet (cross-references, citations, hidden code): that is Milestone 4.
After you re-render it, copy it to docs/index.html again and push, so the report on GitHub Pages stays current (see Milestone 2).



4. Update your environment
Your scripts probably use new packages (click or docopt, a validation package). Add each one, pinned, the same way you did in Milestone 2: add it with uv or renv, commit the changed files and push, let GitHub Actions publish a new image and update the tag in docker-compose.yml, then git pull and docker compose pull. (uv recap from DSCI 521)


5. Update your README
Your README must say how to run each script, in order, with the exact command and its arguments, using the container (docker compose run --rm analysis-env ...), then how to render the report.






Important5 all-or-nothing points for your README instructions



If someone can’t run each of your scripts and render your report by following your instructions exactly as written, you lose all 5 points. Test them on both Windows and Mac. If your team doesn’t have both, ask another team to test them.

text:

TipCheck yourself before submitting

3 Dockerfile
A Dockerfile contains instructions for building a custom Docker image.
Basic structure:
# Start with a base image
FROM base_image:tag

# Copy files
COPY local_path container_path

# Run commands
RUN command

# Set environment variables
ENV VAR_NAME=value

3.1 Code we run in class: Dockerfile practice
We build an image that has our Python packages from uv.lock installed. We work like the textbook suggests: start small, build the image, try the next command inside the container, and only then add it to the Dockerfile.
Step-by-step instructions:

Please first cd to a local folder of your choice, don’t put all files in your home directory!

# Example `cd` command:
cd /Users/skysheng/Desktop/github/dsci522

Make a new folder called demo_docker (or any other name you like), and move into it

mkdir demo_docker
cd demo_docker

Create a uv project with one package. This makes pyproject.toml, .python-version and uv.lock (see the uv cheatsheet for what each file holds).

uv init --bare
uv python pin 3.14
uv add "pandas==3.1.1"

Print out the files to make sure they are correct.

cat pyproject.toml
cat .python-version

Create a Dockerfile using nano (or a GUI like VS Code).

nano Dockerfile

Copy and paste the following code into the Dockerfile. It starts from the official Python image (the same Python version as .python-version), copies the uv program into the image, and copies our three uv files into the folder /home/project.

FROM python:3.14-slim

COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/

WORKDIR /home/project
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./

If you used nano to create this file, you need to press Cntrl + X to attempt exit, by default it will ask you to save the file. Press Y and then press Enter to save the file.


Build the docker image locally:

# Build the docker image locally, with the tag name `testing_cmds`.
# pay attention to the dot at the end of the command!
docker build --tag testing_cmds .

Run the image you just built, and open a terminal inside the container:

docker run --rm -it testing_cmds bash

Inside the container, test the command that installs our packages, and check that it worked. --locked makes uv sync stop with an error if uv.lock does not match pyproject.toml.

uv sync --locked
uv run python -c "import pandas; print(pandas.__version__)"

If the above commands work, exit the container by typing exit.
Update the Dockerfile to include the newly tested command. We also tell uv to put the environment in /opt/venv instead of /home/project/.venv, so it is not hidden when we later mount our project folder over /home/project, and we put /opt/venv/bin first on the PATH, so python means the environment’s Python.

FROM python:3.14-slim

COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/

WORKDIR /home/project

ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./
RUN uv sync --locked
ENV PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH"

Re-build the docker image (same command as step 7), then check that pandas is installed:

docker build --tag testing_cmds .
docker run --rm testing_cmds python -c "import pandas; print(pandas.__version__)"

Iterate through steps 7 to 12 (build the image, run the container’s terminal, test a new command, add it to the Dockerfile, build again …) until you are happy with your Dockerfile.
Use the image with your project folder mounted, so the container can see your files:

docker run --rm -it -v "/$(pwd)":/home/project testing_cmds bash






TipAdding a package later



Add it on your computer with uv add <package>, which updates pyproject.toml and uv.lock, then rebuild the image (step 7).

title: Makefile Cheatsheet
text:
A Makefile consists of rules that tell GNU Make how to build targets. Each rule follows this structure:
target : dependencies
    action
Example:
results/isles.dat : data/isles.txt scripts/wordcount.py
        python scripts/wordcount.py --input_file=data/isles.txt --output_file=results/isles.dat

Target: The name of the file(s) that will be created or updated.

Example: results/isles.dat

Dependencies: Files we need to build the target(s).

includes input files and scripts we will run to output the target(s)
Example: data/isles.txt scripts/wordcount.py
Targets can have 0 or more dependencies

Colon (:) separates targets from dependencies
Action: Commands to run to build or update the target using the dependencies.

Usually shell commands (e.g., running a Python script from command line)
Example: python scripts/wordcount.py --input_file=data/isles.txt --output_file=results/isles.dat
Targets can have zero or more actions

Comments: starting with #







NoteHigh bug zone: TAB required




Actions MUST be indented using the TAB, not spaces!
Depending on which computer you are using, sometimes TAB can still be auto-converted to 4 spaces if you are editing Makefile in VS Code or Jupyter Lab.
🍀 Safest choice: create and edit Makefile in command line using nano or vim from terminal.

2.2 Step 2: Create a Makefile

TODO: Your task is to add a “smarter” data analysis pipeline using GNU Make! It should accomplish the same task as bash runall.sh when you type make all. It should also reset the analysis the starting point (the state when you first copied this repo) when you type make clean.

We will convert every commands in run_all.sh script into rules in Makefile.

2.2.1 First rule in Makefile

We start with converting the following command in run_all.sh script:

python scripts/wordcount.py --input_file=data/isles.txt --output_file=results/isles.dat

Create a new file called Makefile in the root directory:

nano Makefile

Add the following rule (pay attention to TAB indentation):

results/isles.dat : data/isles.txt scripts/wordcount.py
        python scripts/wordcount.py --input_file=data/isles.txt --output_file=results/isles.dat

Save the file above and run the make rule in the terminal:

make results/isles.dat






WarningDebug error: make: Nothing to be done for 'results/isles.dat'.





If you see the following output:
$ make results/isles.dat
make: Nothing to be done for `results/isles.dat'.
This means you are not using the correct TAB indentation. Try edit the Makefile in your terminal and redo all TAB key there.









WarningDebug message: make: 'results/isles.dat' is up to date.





If you succeed the first time you run the command above, but the second time you run the same command, it says:
$ make results/isles.dat
make: `results/isles.dat' is up to date.
This is normal, because your output file already exists, and the timestamp of that output file is more recent than the timestamp of the input file. Makefile will not re-run the command if you did not make any changes to the input file. If you update the timestamp of the input file using touch:
touch data/isles.txt
then rerun make results/isles.dat, it will run again, because now the timestamp of the input file is more recent than the timestamp of the output file, meaning that new changes have been made to the input file after you generated the output file last time.









TipQuestion: Can I call Makefile something else?





Yes you can, for example, if we call it random_name, you will just need to run the following command to generate the target output:
make -f random_name results/isles.dat





2.2.2 Create target and PHONY targets

It’s tedious to always type long file path & name, like results/isles.dat. You can create a target that is a short name for the long file path & name.

result : results/isles.dat

Usually we list those short names as PHONY targets, like this:

.PHONY : result
We use PHONY targets because:

It’s good practice to document and list all your target names in the begining of the Makefile.
If you have a file that is called the same name as a target, PHONY targets will tell GNU Make to ignore the file and use the target instead.


You can also add the clean target to delete everything:

clean:
    rm -f results/isles.dat

We update the Makefile to include new target, PHONY targets, clean target, and add a new rule to create the plot too:

.PHONY : result clean

result : results/isles.dat results/figure/isles.png

# count words
results/isles.dat : data/isles.txt scripts/wordcount.py
        python scripts/wordcount.py --input_file=data/isles.txt --output_file=results/isles.dat

# create the plots
results/figure/isles.png : results/isles.dat scripts/plotcount.py
        python scripts/plotcount.py \
                --input_file=results/isles.dat \
                --output_file=results/figure/isles.png

clean :
        rm -f results/isles.dat results/figure/isles.png

Test out our new Makefile!


Clean everything:

make clean

Would this run? Although we did not create results/isles.dat yet?

make results/figure/isles.png

🤩 Yes it will run! If GNU Make detects that you are missing the input file needed to create the target, it will try to find which rule can create this missing input file, and execute that rule first!
Clean everything again:

make clean

Run all the steps:

make result

# Makefile
# Tiffany Timbers, Nov 2018

# This driver script completes the textual analysis of
# 3 novels and creates figures on the 10 most frequently
# occuring words from each of the 3 novels. This script
# takes no arguments.

# example usage:
# make all

.PHONY: all dats figs clean-dats clean-figs clean-all

# run entire analysis
all: report/count_report.html

# count words
dats: results/isles.dat \
results/abyss.dat \
results/last.dat \
results/sierra.dat

results/isles.dat : scripts/wordcount.py data/isles.txt
    python scripts/wordcount.py \
        --input_file=data/isles.txt \
        --output_file=results/isles.dat
results/abyss.dat : scripts/wordcount.py data/abyss.txt
    python scripts/wordcount.py \
        --input_file=data/abyss.txt \
        --output_file=results/abyss.dat
results/last.dat : scripts/wordcount.py data/last.txt
    python scripts/wordcount.py \
        --input_file=data/last.txt \
        --output_file=results/last.dat
results/sierra.dat : scripts/wordcount.py data/sierra.txt
    python scripts/wordcount.py \
        --input_file=data/sierra.txt \
        --output_file=results/sierra.dat

# plot
figs : results/figure/isles.png \
    results/figure/abyss.png \
    results/figure/last.png \
    results/figure/sierra.png

results/figure/isles.png : scripts/plotcount.py results/isles.dat
    python scripts/plotcount.py \
        --input_file=results/isles.dat \
        --output_file=results/figure/isles.png
results/figure/abyss.png : scripts/plotcount.py results/abyss.dat
    python scripts/plotcount.py \
        --input_file=results/abyss.dat \
        --output_file=results/figure/abyss.png
results/figure/last.png : scripts/plotcount.py results/last.dat
    python scripts/plotcount.py \
        --input_file=results/last.dat \
        --output_file=results/figure/last.png
results/figure/sierra.png : scripts/plotcount.py results/sierra.dat
    python scripts/plotcount.py \
        --input_file=results/sierra.dat \
        --output_file=results/figure/sierra.png

# write the report
report/count_report.html : report/count_report.qmd figs
    quarto render report/count_report.qmd

    rm -f results/isles.dat \
        results/abyss.dat \
        results/last.dat \
        results/sierra.dat

clean-figs :
    rm -f results/figure/isles.png \
    results/figure/abyss.png \
    results/figure/last.png \
    results/figure/sierra.png

clean-all : clean-dats \
    clean-figs

    rm -rf report/count_report_files

2 Start a new project







Task
Command




Create a project (only makes pyproject.toml)
uv init --bare


Choose the Python version (makes .python-version)
uv python pin 3.14


Add a package (updates pyproject.toml and uv.lock, builds .venv/)
uv add pandas


Add a specific version
uv add "pandas==3.1.1"

2.1 Make uv add write exact versions
By default uv add pandas writes "pandas>=3.1.1" (this version or newer) into pyproject.toml. For a data analysis project, add these lines to pyproject.toml so every uv add from now on writes an exact version ("pandas==3.1.1"):
[tool.uv]
add-bounds = "exact"
The setting only changes packages you add after it.

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 1
text:
💥 Consequences of Untested Systems
Untested system for radiation therapy: Terac-25


Source: Cleveland Clinic


The Therac-25 was a radiation therapy machine controlled by software, built by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and used in hospitals in Canada and the United States.
Between 1985 and 1987 it gave at least six patients a massive overdose of radiation, in some cases around 100 times the intended dose. Some patients were badly injured and at least three died.
What went wrong:

Older models had hardware safety locks that physically stopped an overdose. The Therac-25 removed them and trusted the software to do that job.
The software was reused from the older models, written by one programmer, and never properly tested or reviewed by anyone independent.
It had a bug that only showed up when an experienced operator typed quickly and corrected a setting within a few seconds. Slow testers never triggered it.
When it happened, the screen only said “MALFUNCTION 54”. Nobody knew what that meant, the machine showed such messages often, and operators could press one key to continue.
The manufacturer first insisted an overdose was impossible, so the accidents kept happening.

Ask: the code ran, and it worked most of the time. Was that enough?
Takeaway: code that runs is not the same as code we can trust. This is why we write tests in this course.

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 3
text:
Where did cowsay go?
# 1. open a container, install cowsay, check it works
docker run --rm -it python:3.14-slim bash
pip install cowsay
python -c "import cowsay"      # works
exit

# 2. open the same image again
docker run --rm -it python:3.14-slim bash
python -c "import cowsay"
What happens in step 2?

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'cowsay'


Ask the class to guess before revealing. Run it live if there is time (tested: step 2 prints ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'cowsay').
Back to the classroom container from last lecture: the image is the blueprint, a container is one room built from it. Installing cowsay changed the room, not the blueprint. --rm demolished the room. The next docker run builds a fresh room from the same blueprint, without cowsay.
So: if we want cowsay in every room, we have to change the blueprint. That is today.

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 3
section: Change the blueprint, not the room
text:
Change the blueprint, not the room

A Dockerfile is a plain text file with the instructions to build an image
docker build follows it, line by line, and saves the result as an image
Everyone who builds it, or downloads the image, gets the same rooms


Today we walk through Individual Assignment 2 together, step by step.



A Dockerfile is the written list of instructions the builders follow, so anyone can rebuild the same blueprint. Building an image by hand and saving it (docker commit) also exists, but nobody can see what you did. The Dockerfile is transparent: it is in Git, people can read it and review it.

Some data science conventions

Folder and file names: snake_case (lowercase + underscore), no spaces
Documentation (README.md): Markdown. Need a review? Markdown tutorial
Settings and configuration: YAML (.yml or .yaml), not for documentation

Structure comes from indentation with spaces, never tabs

Today we write two YAML files: the GitHub Actions workflow and docker-compose.yml. A tab instead of spaces is the most common reason they break.

How to write a Dockerfile without pain

Pick a base image from Docker Hub, write FROM <base image>
Open a container from it: docker run --rm -it <base image> bash
Try your install commands by hand until they work
Copy the ones that worked into the Dockerfile
docker build after every 2 or 3 new lines
Works on your laptop? Only then move to GitHub Actions


From the textbook chapter “Customizing and building containers”. Debugging a build on GitHub Actions takes minutes per try. Debugging in a container on your laptop takes seconds.
Live, step 2 and 3 (short):

docker run --rm -it ubuntu:24.04 bash
cat /etc/os-release → Ubuntu 24.04.

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 3
text:
Demo: IA2 steps 3 and 4
Follow along on the IA2 page: write the Dockerfile, build it, test it.

IA2 page: step 3, open “The Dockerfile (step 3)” box (uv tab), then step 4, “Commands to test your image (step 4)”.
Writing the Dockerfile:
Live: nano Dockerfile (or code . and make a new file named Dockerfile, no extension), paste the uv version from the IA2 page, save. Then click through the highlights:

FROM: the base image. Ubuntu Linux, no Python. Exact tag, never latest.
COPY --from: copy the uv program out of the image uv publishes. The tag 0.13.7 pins uv’s own version.
WORKDIR: like cd, for the rest of the build and for containers from this image. It creates the folder.
ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT: put the environment in /opt/venv, not in /workspace/.venv. Why: later you mount your project folder over /workspace with -v, and a mount hides whatever was there. Worse, uv would find your laptop’s .venv and replace it with a Linux one.
COPY: only the three files that list the packages. Not your code, not .venv/. Ask: why not just copy .venv/? Because on a Mac, file .venv/bin/python3 says Mach-O 64-bit executable arm64, a program that does not run on Linux. And uv.lock is enough to rebuild the same versions inside the image. Same as last lecture: the shopping list and the receipt travel, the electronics are bought again where you land.
RUN uv sync --locked: runs during the build. Installs Python 3.14 and exactly the versions in uv.lock.

Build and test:
Terminal, step by step:

docker build --tag dsci522-test . → point at the dot: “build from this folder” (the build context, where COPY finds the files). --tag names the image. Point at the steps [1/5] to [5/5], one per line of the Dockerfile. It takes about 7 seconds.
docker images dsci522-test → about 386 MB.
The test command from the slide → a cow says “numpy says 1 + 2 + 3 = 6”. If a package were missing, it would be a ModuleNotFoundError instead.
Look around: docker run --rm -it dsci522-test bash

ls -a → only .python-version, pyproject.toml, uv.lock. No .venv.
python3 --version → still command not found: Python is not on the PATH.
uv run which python → /opt/venv/bin/python. uv knows where the environment is.
exit

docker history dsci522-test | head -7 → one row per line of the Dockerfile, newest on top. RUN uv sync is about 147 MB, ENV is 0B. These rows are the layers: next slide.

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 3
section: Each line is a layer, and layers are reused
text:
Each line is a layer, and layers are reused

Docker saves the result of each line as a layer
Rebuild: a line whose input did not change says CACHED and is reused
Change one line, and that line and every line below it run again
So: things that change rarely go at the top, things that change often at the bottom


Live: add a CMD line at the bottom of the Dockerfile:
CMD ["uv", "run", "python", "-c", "import cowsay; cowsay.cow('Moo from my image')"]

docker build --tag dsci522-test . → steps 2 to 5 all say CACHED, the build takes about a second.
docker run --rm dsci522-test → no command after the image name, so the CMD runs: “Moo from my image”.
CMD is the default command. A command after the image name replaces it (like bash did earlier).

Remove the CMD line again afterwards, so the Dockerfile matches the assignment (the CMD is not wrong, just not needed).
This is why we copy only the three uv files, not the whole folder: editing a script does not reinstall the packages.

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 3
text:
What --locked protects you from
Someone types "pandas==3.1.1" into pyproject.toml by hand, without uv add:
 => ERROR [stage-0 5/5] RUN uv sync --locked
error: The lockfile at `uv.lock` needs to be updated, but `--locked` was provided.
hint: To update the lockfile, run `uv lock`.


Without --locked, uv would quietly make a new lock file inside the image
The image would no longer match the uv.lock in your repository
Fix: uv lock, then commit pyproject.toml and uv.lock together

docker build --tag dsci522-test . → the error on the slide.

docker build --tag dsci522-test . → works again.

🦦 Greet otters using click!

"""Otter Greeting Generator

This script allows you to greet otters with different levels of enthusiasm.
"""

import click

@click.command()
@click.option('--count', default=1, help='Number of otter greetings.')
@click.option('--name', prompt='Your name', help='The person to greet.')
@click.option('--enthusiasm', type=click.Choice(['low', 'medium', 'high']), 
              default='medium', help='How enthusiastic should the otters be?')
def greet_otters(count, name, enthusiasm):
    """ Otter greeting generator
    
    Simple program that has adorable otters greet NAME for COUNT times. 🦦
    
    Parameters
    ----------
    count : int
        Number of otter greetings to display. Must be a positive integer.
        Default is 1.
    name : str
        The name of the person to greet. Will be prompted if not provided
        via command line.
    enthusiasm : {'low', 'medium', 'high'}
        The enthusiasm level of the otter greetings:
        - 'low': Simple, calm greeting
        - 'medium': Friendly greeting with some emojis
        - 'high': Very excited greeting with lots of emojis and caps
        Default is 'medium'.
    
    Returns
    -------
    None
        Outputs greetings directly to the console using click.echo().
    
    Examples
    --------
    Run from command line:
    
    >>> python otter_greeting.py --name "Oyster" --count 3 --enthusiasm high
    
    This will display 3 highly enthusiastic otter greetings for Oyster.
    """
    # Different enthusiasm levels
    emojis = {
        'low': '🦦',
        'medium': '🦦✨',
        'high': '🦦🎉🌊'
    }
    
    messages = {
        'low': f"hello {name}.",
        'medium': f"Hello {name}! 🌊",
        'high': f"HELLO {name.upper()}!!! Who is that lovely, amazing, genius friend over there?? The otters are SO excited to see you! 🎊"
    }
    
    click.echo(f"\n{emojis[enthusiasm]} Otter Greetings Incoming! {emojis[enthusiasm]}\n")
    
    for i in range(count):
        click.echo(f"  Otter #{i+1}: {messages[enthusiasm]}")
    
    click.echo(f"\n🦦 You've been greeted by {count} friendly otter(s)! 🦦\n")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    greet_otters()

--name=<name>      Your name (the person to greet)
--count=<count>    Number of otter greetings [default: 1]
" -> doc

library(docopt)

opt <- docopt(doc)

main <- function(name, count) {
  # Convert count to numeric (docopt returns strings)
  count <- as.numeric(count)
  
  # Generate otter greetings
  cat("\n🦦 Otter Greetings Incoming! 🦦\n\n")
  
  for (i in 1:count) {
    cat(paste0("  Otter #", i, ": Hello ", name, "! 🌊\n"))
  }
  
  cat(paste0("\n🦦 You've been greeted by ", count, " friendly otter(s)! 🦦\n\n"))
}

main(opt$name, opt$count)
